extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, policymakers, and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how news and public discourse should be framed and produced to enlist interest, avoid common cognitive and statistical errors, and match temporal and visual perspective to the public's capacity to understand and act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match time-conception to the thing at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: An important part of wisdom is the ability to distinguish the time-conception that properly belongs to the thing in hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to calculate for the emergency or for the long run; some decisions require hours, others decades or centuries. Use the time-perspective appropriate to the practical purpose (e.g., salvaging civilization vs long-term future of mankind).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid immortalizing policy beyond reason (resist mortmain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions, wills, or other instruments ought not to make rules and restrictions more permanent than ordinary statutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits to imposing one's moral stencil on unknown future generations; prefer amendability and humility about the future when drafting enduring rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an appropriate posterity horizon for resource and policy decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When computing social policy about exhaustible resources or long-term investments, determine how far into the future 'posterity' should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Square computations of reserves, rates of use, and alternative fuels with an explicit standard of time (e.g., grandchildren vs great-grandchildren vs 100 years) and treat restoration of balance as a charge upon the future when emergencies arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using time-perspective to excuse inertia or injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use long-range demographic arguments or other temporal calculations to justify present inaction or immoral choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: saying mass deaths don't matter because future birthrates will replace them is misuse of time perspective; similarly, buying short-term peace that endangers future generations is improper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer statistically sound sampling (use random/neutral methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: To pick fairly a good sample of a large class you must use neutral, accidental, or random methods rather than convenience samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: Sheffield social workers were advised to use at least 408 men and 408 women selected by a random method; avoid selecting respondents from one's contacts or from institutions that bias results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selection bias and cherry-picking of samples
rubrics_metrics.description: The casual mind tends to pick samples that support its prejudices; such selections produce worthless, unrepresentative results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of evidence drawn from the most troublesome or most docile examples; do not treat small or convenient subgroups as representative of whole classes (e.g., equating organized trade unionists with all 'Labor').

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about classification limits and how groups are defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations about classes (e.g., 'the working class') cover only part of the truth at particular times and may exclude many who slip out of the net.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appealing to or describing a class, specify who is included and who is not (farm hands, clerks, small shopkeepers, etc.), and avoid tacitly endowing the whole class with the point of view of an organized nucleus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring causation from mere sequence or association
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonest form of reasoning is intuitive post hoc ergo propter hoc; sequence or parallelism is not equivalent to cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large public issues rarely have obvious causes; be cautious in attributing causal links from coincident events and seek rigorous investigation rather than intuitive leaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against emotion-driven associative reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful feelings attached to one idea tend to pull into the same causal system other ideas that feel similar, even if unrelated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: attributing smallpox outbreaks to alehouses or linking scientific theories to political unrest. Excavate emotional entanglements and test actual links rather than relying on affective associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid absolutist language; use qualifiers where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: People prefer absolutes and dislike qualifying adverbs, but nearly every public-affairs opinion needs qualifying words (rather, perhaps, if, but, partly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deflate absolutist claims with moderation; remember results and effects are often relative rather than universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate abstract ideas into visual or tactile forms for public lucidity
rubrics_metrics.description: No idea is lucid for practical decision until it has visual or tactile value; visualization helps make ideas real to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since intuitions are private and hard to communicate, render them into images, metaphors, or concrete examples so a number of people can grasp and act on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictures and imagery to convey ideas effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea, and words that call up pictures are next best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular representation benefits when a gifted visualizer translates abstractions into moving pictures (stories, cartoons, films) so audiences can identify and participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personify institutions and abstractions carefully to aid comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: We tend to dramatize relations and personalize quantities by treating institutions (e.g., 'England') as persons like John Bull.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personification makes complex issues comprehensible but is porous and can introduce old meanings; use it to simplify while being mindful of distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make protagonists and antagonists clear in popular storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation, the handles for identification are almost always marked: you know who the hero is at once; works without definite marking are unlikely to be popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For news stories aimed at mass audiences, clearly signal actors, stakes, and conflicts so the audience can quickly identify whom to support or oppose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the audience something to do—provide engagement or exercise of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must have something to do; contemplation of ideals alone is not activity. To prevent passive viewing, the image must exercise the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stories that invite participation, mobilize feelings, or offer actionable angles rather than mere abstract exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use compelling motifs (fighting and sexual passion) cautiously to arouse interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Two forms of exercise most easily arouse interest are sexual passion and fighting; the fighting motif dominates politics and makes issues popular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While these motifs are powerful for engagement, their cultural prominence varies (e.g., sexual motif less used in American political imagery). Employ them only when relevant and ethically appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selecting historical periods to suit present arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments from history often select past dates that support the speaker's present view; the same territory can be framed as belonging to different groups depending on chosen dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about the temporal frame when invoking history (e.g., Alsace-Lorraine can be framed many ways); acknowledge alternative historical starting points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence training and responsibility appropriately in proposals for institutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs that shift responsibility (e.g., industrial democratization) must align the assumption of responsibility with a complementary program of training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid proposals that expect instant competence (sudden dictatorship of the proletariat) or deny time for capacity-building; ensure reform plans include realistic time for acquiring skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor policy and mandates to the developmental stage of peoples or communities
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of mandates must differ according to the stage of development of the people; time conception influences relations between mandatories and the mandated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should recognize varying stages and avoid treating 'backwardness' as intrinsic; successful mandating involves programs with definite standards and estimates of time.
